title: Dwarf galaxies kept only a tenth of the oxygen their stars made
freshness: Peer-reviewed paper published in The Astrophysical Journal on November 2, 2026; selected within the preferred 15-day window.
excerpt: A census of 37 nearby dwarf galaxies found that they retain only 4% to 25% of the oxygen their stars produced, with an average near 11%. Most of the missing oxygen may have been swept out by stellar winds and supernovae, but its present location is still unknown.
whyItMatters: Oxygen tracks how stars enrich galaxies and the space around them. Finding far less oxygen than simulations predict shows that feedback in small galaxies may remove material more efficiently than current models capture.

body:
## An oxygen account that does not balance

Thirty-seven nearby dwarf galaxies are missing most of the oxygen their stars should have made. A new census finds that these small, gas-rich galaxies retain between about 4% and 25% of their produced oxygen. The sample average is just 10.7%.

Oxygen is built inside massive stars and released when those stars shed material or explode. Astronomers use it as a practical tracer for other heavy elements because it is abundant, its production is comparatively well understood, and its signature can be measured in interstellar gas. If researchers can estimate how much oxygen a galaxy's stars made and count how much remains, the difference records how matter has moved through and beyond the galaxy.

The Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds project, called GLOW, applied that accounting to star-forming dwarf galaxies within 6 megaparsecs, or about 20 million light-years. Their stellar masses range from roughly 3 million to 3 billion Suns. All are close enough for Hubble to resolve individual stars, which lets the team reconstruct when each galaxy formed stars and how its chemical composition changed.

## Counting what was made and what remains

The researchers combined Hubble measurements with infrared observations from Spitzer, neutral-hydrogen maps from the Very Large Array and Australian Telescope Compact Array, and published spectroscopy. Stellar mass and star-formation histories provided an estimate of the oxygen forged over each galaxy's lifetime. Gas masses and oxygen abundances measured the largest present reservoir. The team also estimated the smaller amounts locked in stars, stellar remnants, and dust.

The gap was large across the sample. Twenty-nine of the 37 galaxies retained no more than 15% of their produced oxygen. The individual estimates ranged from 3.8% to 24.8%, with a sample standard deviation of 5.1 percentage points. Nearly all oxygen that did remain was in interstellar gas rather than stars or dust.

Those percentages are reconstructed budgets, not a direct inventory of every oxygen atom. They depend on stellar-yield calculations, inferred star-formation histories, gas measurements, dust corrections, and assumptions about the relation between oxygen and iron. The researchers propagated those uncertainties and repeated part of the analysis with two stellar-evolution libraries. The basic shortage persisted.

## Winds are the likely exit route

Dwarf galaxies have shallow gravitational wells. Energy from massive stars and supernovae can drive enriched gas outward more easily than in a large galaxy. This process, known as stellar feedback, makes galactic winds the leading explanation for the missing oxygen. The result suggests that these winds remove metals more efficiently than current hydrodynamical simulations predict, even though those simulations reproduce the familiar relation between a galaxy's mass and metallicity.

The study does not show where the oxygen is now. Ultraviolet observations have detected ionized oxygen in the circumgalactic medium, the diffuse halo surrounding a galaxy. The directly traced ion accounts for only about 1% to 7% of the oxygen produced. Correcting for unseen ionization states could raise the halo share to roughly 5% to 35%, but that correction is uncertain. Much of the oxygen may still be in a hard-to-detect halo phase, or it may have escaped into intergalactic space.

**Measured:** 37 nearby, gas-rich dwarf galaxies retain a small fraction of the oxygen their stars produced, averaging 10.7%.

**Inferred:** past stellar winds and supernovae probably removed most of it, but its final destination remains open.
